name: Competitive biohacking

lead: Competitive biohacking is the practice of ranking one's health or ageing measurements against those of other people, for example on a leaderboard of biological-age scores. It sits within the wider biohacking and longevity movement, where people track biomarkers and adjust diet, exercise, sleep and supplements.

The appearance link is indirect: the habits people compete on, such as sleep, training, body composition and sun and skin care, are the same ones associated with looking healthier and younger. The best-known public example is entrepreneur Bryan Johnson, who has said he started competing against others in 2023 after a suggestion from a colleague.

paras: Participants measure markers such as DNA-methylation ageing pace, body composition, blood panels and fitness tests, share or compare them, and treat standing on a leaderboard as motivation. In forums such as T Nation, related comparisons appear in discussions of body composition measured by hydrostatic weighing.

Biological-age tests are research tools and experts quoted in press coverage have questioned how much current science can promise. Highly intensive regimens may involve cost, many supplements or procedures; critics cite examples such as plasma transfusions, which the FDA has said offer no proven benefit and may be harmful. Comparison itself can add pressure.

angle.text: People use the competitive element to stay consistent with habits tied to a fitter, younger look. The ranking itself does not change appearance; the behaviour it motivates may.

lead: Competitive biohacking is a form of biohacking in which people compare their health, fitness or ageing measurements with others and treat the ranking as a goal. Biohacking is a broad term covering quantified-self tracking, nutrition and supplement experimentation, and do-it-yourself biology [1].

The most visible example is Bryan Johnson, the entrepreneur behind the Blueprint longevity protocol. Wikipedia reports that since 2023 he has engaged in competitive biohacking against others, an idea recommended by his Blueprint co-founder Kate Tolo, and that a July 2024 Times article described a biohacking leaderboard on which another person ranked ahead of him [2]. He tracks more than 100 measurements and has published a DunedinPACE score, a DNA-methylation estimate of the pace of ageing [2].
For looksmaxxing, the connection is the underlying habits: sleep, training, body composition and general health, which affect how fit, lean and youthful someone looks.
infobox: Biological age (e.g. DunedinPACE), biomarkers, body composition [2]

paras: Biohacking, as a term, can refer to quantified-self tracking, nutrition and supplement experimentation, body modification, do-it-yourself biology and genetic techniques [1]. The competitive variant adds comparison with peers, usually on measures of ageing or physical condition.

Johnson announced Project Blueprint in October 2021 with the stated goal of reducing the biological age of his organs, and the protocol reportedly cost about 2 million dollars a year in 2023 [2]. By 2024 Blueprint was selling a monthly subscription and had raised 60 million dollars [2].

Press and academic comments have been mixed. McGill pharmacologist Moshe Szyf doubted that science can yet deliver the results Johnson claims, and researcher Andrew Steele said none of his practices can change his genes [2]. The FDA has said plasma transfusions, one of his reported procedures, have no benefit and may be harmful; Johnson later said he would not repeat them [2].

Body-composition comparison is a long-running theme on lifting forums. A 2013 T Nation thread titled 'Think You Are Big But Just Fat' includes a member describing a hydrostatic weighing done to compare his build against his own estimates [3]. Discussions of fat-soluble vitamins on the same forum show the supplement-optimisation side of the culture [4].
